metadata.title: Anesthesia Question Bank
metadata.description: Anesthesia multiple-choice questions organized by lecture: preoperative evaluation, monitoring, inhalational and intravenous agents, local anesthetics, neuraxial blockade, airway management, and neuromuscular blockers.

questions.question: A 73-year-old male with a history of hypertension, coronary artery disease, and ischemic cardiomyopathy presents to the preoperative clinic for risk assessment prior to an elective open repair of an infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm. His home medications include lisinopril, carvedilol, and atorvastatin. On physical examination, blood pressure is 152/88 mmHg, pulse is 82/min and regular, and respiratory rate is 16/min. Jugular venous distension is noted at 6 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees. Cardiac auscultation reveals a low-frequency, dull third heart sound (S3) at the apex during early diastole, along with mild bilateral bibasilar crackles. An electrocardiogram demonstrates normal sinus rhythm with non-specific ST-segment changes. According to the Goldman Cardiac Risk Index for non-cardiac surgery, which of the following findings carries the single highest statistical weight for predicting major perioperative cardiac morbidity and mortality in this patient?

options.A: Age greater than 70 years
options.B: Elevated systolic blood pressure of 152 mmHg
options.C: Intraperitoneal / aortic vascular surgery
options.D: Third heart sound (S3 gallop) and jugular venous distension
options.E: History of coronary artery disease

questions.explanation:
The Goldman Cardiac Risk Index was established to evaluate the risk of major adverse cardiac events (myocardial infarction, pulmonary edema, ventricular fibrillation, cardiac arrest, complete heart block) in patients undergoing non-cardiac surgical procedures. Among all 9 clinical criteria evaluated in the Goldman index, the presence of a third heart sound (S3 gallop) or jugular venous distension (JVD) carries 11 points, representing the single highest statistical predictor of perioperative cardiac death and congestive heart failure decompensation.

An S3 gallop is generated by rapid, passive ventricular filling into a stiff, non-compliant, or volume-overloaded ventricle, indicating high left ventricular end-diastolic pressure and active congestive heart failure. Operating on patients with uncompensated heart failure carries catastrophic mortality. The patient must be medically optimized (e.g., diuretics, afterload reduction) prior to any non-emergent surgical intervention.

High-Yield: Goldman Criteria Point Weight Summary
S3 Gallop / Elevated JVD (11 pts) > Recent MI <6 months (10 pts) > Non-sinus rhythm or PACs (7 pts) = >5 PVCs/min (7 pts) > Age >70 (5 pts) > Emergency operation (4 pts) > Severe Aortic Stenosis (3 pts) = Intraperitoneal/ Intrathoracic/Aortic Surgery (3 pts) = Poor general medical condition (3 pts). Total: 53 points.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. Age > 70 years is an independent variable on the Goldman index, but it is assigned 5 points (significantly lower than S3/JVD at 11 points and recent MI at 10 points).
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Uncontrolled systolic hypertension is NOT an element of the Goldman Cardiac Risk Index. This is one of the classic exam traps; while severe hypertension (≥180/110) warrants medical management, it awards 0 Goldman points.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect. Intraperitoneal, intrathoracic, or aortic procedures carry heightened surgical stress and fluid shifts, but this variable contributes only 3 points to the Goldman score.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. In the Goldman Cardiac Risk Index for non-cardiac surgery, signs of congestive heart failure—specifically a third heart sound (S3 gallop) or jugular venous distension—carry the highest risk weighting (11 points), surpassing even recent myocardial infarction (10 points).
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. A general history of CAD is not directly scored on the Goldman index; rather, a documented recent myocardial infarction within 6 months is specifically scored and awards 10 points.

questions.educationalObjective: In the Goldman Cardiac Risk Index for non-cardiac surgery, signs of congestive heart failure—specifically a third heart sound (S3 gallop) or jugular venous distension—carry the highest risk weighting (11 points), surpassing even recent myocardial infarction (10 points).

questions.question: A 29-year-old primigravida at 38 weeks gestation presents to the labor and delivery triage unit in active labor. Her prenatal course has been uncomplicated. She has no chronic medical conditions, takes only prenatal vitamins, and has no prior surgical history. Her vital signs are: blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse 80/min, respiratory rate 14/min, and temperature 37.0°C (98.6°F). BMI is 27 kg/m<sup>2</sup>. Cervical examination demonstrates 5 cm dilation and 80% effacement. She requests labor epidural analgesia. According to the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status classification system, which of the following represents this patient's correct classification?

options.A: ASA I
options.B: ASA II
options.C: ASA III
options.D: ASA IV
options.E: ASA I E

questions.explanation:
The American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) Physical Status classification is used worldwide to grade preoperative physical fitness and systemic illness. An otherwise completely healthy, non-morbidly obese pregnant woman is automatically classified as ASA Class II.

Pregnancy induces profound physiological alterations across virtually every organ system, including an expanded intravascular blood volume (30–50%), increased cardiac output, reduced functional residual capacity (FRC) by 20%, increased oxygen consumption, and delayed gastric emptying with elevated intra-abdominal pressure (heightened risk of pulmonary aspiration). Because these physiological alterations deviate significantly from non-pregnant baseline homeostasis, normal pregnancy constitutes mild systemic physiological perturbation without functional incapacity, perfectly matching the definition of ASA II.

High-Yield: Automatic ASA II Classifications
Even without any underlying medical illness, the following patients are automatically classified as ASA II: (1) Healthy pregnant women, (2) Current cigarette smokers, (3) Social alcohol drinkers, (4) Mildly obese individuals (BMI 30–39.9 kg/m2), and (5) Patients aged >80 years.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. ASA Class I is strictly reserved for normal, healthy patients with no organic, physiologic, or psychiatric disease processes. Pregnancy precludes an ASA I designation due to inherent systemic adaptations.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A healthy pregnant woman is classified as ASA Class II due to the significant normal physiological alterations of pregnancy (decreased FRC, increased cardiac output, delayed gastric emptying).
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect. ASA Class III denotes severe systemic illness that imposes definite functional limitations on daily physical activity (e.g., poorly controlled pre-eclampsia, gestational diabetes with end-organ damage, symptomatic valve lesions).
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. ASA Class IV denotes severe systemic disease that is a constant, ongoing threat to life (e.g., eclampsia with pulmonary edema, peripartum cardiomyopathy with ejection fraction <20%).
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. An emergency designation ('E') is reserved for acute surgical interventions where delay would significantly increase threat to life or limb (e.g., emergent cesarean delivery for umbilical cord prolapse or uterine rupture). Normal labor epidural placement is an elective analgesic service.

questions.educationalObjective: A healthy pregnant woman is classified as ASA Class II due to the significant normal physiological alterations of pregnancy (decreased FRC, increased cardiac output, delayed gastric emptying).

questions.question: A 45-year-old female presents for pre-anesthetic airway evaluation prior to elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. The resident physician explains the procedure for evaluating the oropharyngeal anatomy using the modified Mallampati classification system. Which of the following describes the correct positioning and maneuver required to obtain an accurate, valid Mallampati score?

options.A: Supine position, mouth opened maximally, tongue resting inside the mouth with sustained phonation ("saying ah")
options.B: Sitting upright, mouth opened partially, tongue protruded with phonation
options.C: Sitting upright, mouth opened maximally, tongue protruded maximally WITHOUT phonation
options.D: Standing position, mouth opened maximally, tongue protruded with phonation
options.E: Semi-Fowler position, head fully extended, tongue resting on the floor of the mouth without phonation

questions.explanation:
The Mallampati classification assesses the size of the tongue base relative to the capacity of the oropharyngeal cavity. To maintain strict standardization and inter-rater reliability, the examination MUST be performed with the patient:
1. Seated in an upright posture with eyes level with the examiner.
2. Opening the mouth maximally.
3. Protruding the tongue as far forward as possible.
4. WITHOUT PHONATION (instructing the patient to breathe quietly without saying "ah").

Phonation causes voluntary contraction of the tensor and levator veli palatini muscles, which artificially elevates the soft palate and widens the faucial pillars. This produces an artificial, falsely favorable lower score (e.g., masking an underlying Mallampati Class III or IV airway as a Class I or II), leading to dangerous underestimation of intubation difficulty.

High-Yield: Mallampati Anatomical Structures Checklist
Class I: PUSH (Pillars, Uvula, Soft palate, Hard palate). Class II: USH (Uvula, Soft palate, Hard palate — pillars hidden). Class III: SH (Soft palate, Hard palate — only base of uvula visible). Class IV: H (Hard palate ONLY visible — high risk of difficult laryngoscopy!).

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. All these choices include incorrect patient posture (supine, semi-Fowler, standing), incorrect tongue position (resting inside the mouth, partially open mouth), or the major error of phonation.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. All these choices include incorrect patient posture (supine, semi-Fowler, standing), incorrect tongue position (resting inside the mouth, partially open mouth), or the major error of phonation.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. To accurately perform the Mallampati airway assessment, the patient must be seated upright, open the mouth maximally, and protrude the tongue forward without phonation. Phonation artificially elevates the soft palate and creates a false-negative assessment.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. All these choices include incorrect patient posture (supine, semi-Fowler, standing), incorrect tongue position (resting inside the mouth, partially open mouth), or the major error of phonation.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. All these choices include incorrect patient posture (supine, semi-Fowler, standing), incorrect tongue position (resting inside the mouth, partially open mouth), or the major error of phonation.

questions.educationalObjective: To accurately perform the Mallampati airway assessment, the patient must be seated upright, open the mouth maximally, and protrude the tongue forward without phonation. Phonation artificially elevates the soft palate and creates a false-negative assessment.

questions.question: A 22-year-old male from Irbid undergoes emergency reduction of an open femur fracture under general anesthesia. Induction is performed with intravenous propofol and succinylcholine, followed by endotracheal intubation. Maintenance of anesthesia is established with sevoflurane in an oxygen/nitrous oxide mixture. Twenty minutes into the procedure, the anesthesiologist notes that the end-tidal CO<sub>2</sub> (ETCO<sub>2</sub>) has risen acutely from 36 mmHg to 68 mmHg, despite doubling the mechanical minute ventilation from 5 L/min to 10 L/min. Heart rate increases from 75/min to 135/min, and blood pressure rises to 165/95 mmHg. Examination of the limbs reveals generalized skeletal muscle rigidity. A rectal temperature probe records a core temperature of 38.8°C (101.8°F), which increases by 0.5°C over the subsequent 3 minutes. Which of the following represents the earliest, most sensitive pathognomonic indicator of this syndrome?

options.A: Marked hyperthermia (>40°C)
options.B: Severe sinus tachycardia
options.C: Unexplained, rapid elevation in end-tidal CO<sub>2</sub> (ETCO<sub>2</sub>)
options.D: Dark brown myoglobinuria
options.E: Masseter muscle spasm during laryngoscopy

questions.explanation:
This clinical vignette portrays a classic presentation of acute Malignant Hyperthermia (MH), an autosomal dominant pharmacogenetic channelopathy triggered by exposure to volatile inhalational anesthetics (halothane, sevoflurane, isoflurane, desflurane) and the depolarizing muscle relaxant succinylcholine. The earliest, most reliable, and most sensitive indicator of malignant hyperthermia in an intubated, mechanically ventilated patient is an acute, unexplained rise in End-Tidal Carbon Dioxide (ETCO2) that is refractory to massive increases in minute ventilation. This occurs because the primary underlying cellular defect (uncontrolled calcium efflux via mutated RYR1 receptors in the sarcoplasmic reticulum) drives uncontrolled, runaway aerobic and anaerobic metabolism in skeletal muscle, generating enormous quantities of CO2 and heat.

High-Yield: Immediate Management of Malignant Hyperthermia
1. STOP triggering agents immediately (vaporizers off, discontinue succinylcholine). 2. Hyperventilate with 100% O2 at maximum flow rates (≥10 L/min). 3. Administer IV Dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg rapid IV push; repeat every 5–10 minutes up to 10 mg/kg until hypermetabolism is arrested. 4. Initiate active cooling (cold IV saline, surface ice packs); stop at ≤38.5°C to prevent hypothermic overshoot. 5. Administer IV sodium bicarbonate for severe metabolic acidosis and treat hyperkalemia.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. Severe hyperthermia is a late sign of malignant hyperthermia! Relying on fever to diagnose MH will lead to delayed treatment and fatal outcomes. Core temperature can rise dramatically (>1°C every 5 minutes up to >42°C), but this occurs after the hypermetabolic surge is already advanced.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Tachycardia is an early and frequent compensatory sign of sympathetic activation, hypercapnia, and metabolic surge, but it is non-specific (commonly caused by light anesthesia, pain, or hypovolemia).
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The earliest and most sensitive indicator of malignant hyperthermia during general anesthesia is a rapid, unexplained elevation in end-tidal CO<sub>2</sub> (ETCO<sub>2</sub>) that persists despite aggressive hyperventilation. Hyperthermia is a dangerous late manifestation.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. Myoglobinuria (dark red-brown urine) and acute renal failure result from extensive rhabdomyolysis and muscle necrosis; this is a late complication.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. Masseter muscle spasm occurs specifically following succinylcholine administration at induction in ~50% of cases, but ETCO<sub>2</sub> elevation remains the primary pathognomonic safety monitor in ventilated patients.

questions.educationalObjective: The earliest and most sensitive indicator of malignant hyperthermia during general anesthesia is a rapid, unexplained elevation in end-tidal CO<sub>2</sub> (ETCO<sub>2</sub>) that persists despite aggressive hyperventilation. Hyperthermia is a dangerous late manifestation.

questions.question: A 2-year-old previously healthy boy is scheduled for elective bilateral myringotomy and tympanostomy tube placement under general anesthesia at 10:00 AM. Upon arrival at 8:00 AM, the mother reports that the child was crying and hungry at 6:00 AM (2 hours prior to arrival), and she fed him a bottle containing 150 mL of commercial infant formula milk. The child has no history of gastroesophageal reflux or delayed gastric emptying. According to the ASA Preoperative Fasting Guidelines, which of the following is the most appropriate management plan regarding the timing of his surgery?

options.A: Proceed with surgery at 10:00 AM because infant formula requires a 4-hour fasting interval
options.B: Proceed with surgery immediately under rapid sequence induction with cricoid pressure
options.C: Postpone the scheduled procedure and wait an additional 4 hours (until 12:00 PM) before proceeding
options.D: Postpone the procedure and wait an additional 6 hours (until 2:00 PM)
options.E: Cancel the procedure and reschedule for another day because any non-clear liquid requires an 8-hour fast

questions.explanation:
Preoperative fasting guidelines established by the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) are designed to minimize the residual gastric volume and acidity at the time of anesthesia induction, mitigating the catastrophic risk of pulmonary aspiration (Mendelson's syndrome).

According to ASA NPO Guidelines:
• Clear liquids: Minimum 2 hours.
• Breast milk: Minimum 4 hours.
• Infant formula, non-human milk, or light non-fat meal: Minimum 6 hours.
• Heavy meal (fried/fatty foods or meat): Minimum 8 hours.

In this case, the child consumed commercial infant formula at 6:00 AM. An infant formula fast requires a total of 6 hours. Because 2 hours have already elapsed at 8:00 AM, the team must wait an additional 4 hours (until 12:00 PM / 6 hours total from ingestion) before proceeding with elective anesthesia induction.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. A 4-hour fasting window applies strictly to breast milk, which is digested and emptied much faster than bovine-based or commercial infant formulas.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Performing rapid sequence induction (RSI) to bypass fasting guidelines is strictly indicated for emergency operations where surgical delay threatens life or limb. For an elective minor procedure, violating NPO guidelines is unacceptable practice.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Under ASA NPO guidelines, the mandatory minimum fasting intervals are: 2 hours for clear liquids, 4 hours for breast milk, 6 hours for infant formula or light meals, and 8 hours for heavy, fatty meals.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. Waiting an additional 6 hours would create an 8-hour total fasting interval, which is only mandated after a heavy, fatty, or meat-containing meal.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. There is no clinical indication to cancel the procedure for another date; delaying by 4 hours within the same surgical day fulfills safety criteria.

questions.educationalObjective: Under ASA NPO guidelines, the mandatory minimum fasting intervals are: 2 hours for clear liquids, 4 hours for breast milk, 6 hours for infant formula or light meals, and 8 hours for heavy, fatty meals.

questions.question: A 58-year-old male with a 35-pack-year smoking history is seen in the preoperative assessment clinic 10 days prior to elective open hemicolectomy for colon adenocarcinoma. He successfully stopped cigarette smoking exactly 1 week (7 days) ago upon being scheduled for surgery. He asks the anesthesiologist what physiological benefits have occurred in his lungs and cardiovascular system during this 1-week period of abstinence. Which of the following physiological changes is most expected in this patient after 1 to 2 weeks of smoking cessation?

options.A: Normalization of systemic immune response and wound healing capacity
options.B: Full restoration of forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV<sub>1</sub>) and vital capacity
options.C: Marked reduction in tracheobronchial secretions and sputum production
options.D: Statistically significant 50% decrease in postoperative pneumonia rates
options.E: Complete reversal of airway hyperreactivity to baseline non-smoker levels

questions.explanation:
Cigarette smoke contains thousands of noxious compounds, including carbon monoxide (CO), nicotine, and hydrogen cyanide, which impair mucociliary transport, paralyze respiratory cilia, increase goblet cell hypertrophy, and generate copious secretions.

The physiological timeline of smoking cessation follows a well-characterized sequence:
• 12–24 Hours: Rapid elimination of nicotine and carbon monoxide; carboxyhemoglobin drops and tissue oxygen delivery improves.
• 48–72 Hours: Complete normalization of carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) levels and rightward restoration of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve (P50).
• 1–2 Weeks: Marked reduction in tracheobronchial secretions, mucous hypersecretion, and sputum volume, accompanied by initial recovery of ciliary beat frequency.
• 4–6 Weeks: Measurable improvements in pulmonary function tests (FEV1, FVC) and closure capacity.
• 6–8 Weeks: Normalization of immune function, bactericidal activity of alveolar macrophages, and collagen deposition.
• 8–12 Weeks: Statistically significant reduction in overall postoperative pulmonary complications (pneumonia, prolonged mechanical ventilation).

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. Normalization of systemic cell-mediated immune function and wound healing takes at least 6 to 8 weeks.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Significant improvements in spirometric parameters (FEV<sub>1</sub> and FVC) require 4 to 6 weeks of sustained abstinence.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Preoperative smoking cessation for 1 to 2 weeks primarily leads to decreased tracheobronchial mucous hypersecretion and reduced sputum volume. Overall reduction in postoperative pulmonary complication rates requires at least 8 weeks of abstinence.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. Meaningful reductions in overall postoperative pulmonary morbidity and pneumonia require at least 8 weeks of preoperative cessation.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. Airway hyperreactivity paradoxically transiently increases during the first few days as the cough reflex awakens; full recovery takes 6–8 weeks.

questions.educationalObjective: Preoperative smoking cessation for 1 to 2 weeks primarily leads to decreased tracheobronchial mucous hypersecretion and reduced sputum volume. Overall reduction in postoperative pulmonary complication rates requires at least 8 weeks of abstinence.

questions.question: A 62-year-old female with a 10-year history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, essential hypertension, and stable angina pectoris presents for preoperative evaluation prior to an elective total hip arthroplasty. Her current daily medications include metformin 1000 mg twice daily, empagliflozin 10 mg once daily, metoprolol succinate 50 mg once daily, and atorvastatin 40 mg once daily. Her baseline serum creatinine is 1.1 mg/dL, and HbA<sub>1c</sub> is 7.2%. Which of the following is the most appropriate perioperative management plan regarding her home medications?

options.A: Discontinue metoprolol on the morning of surgery to prevent severe intraoperative bradycardia
options.B: Continue metformin up to and including the morning of surgery with a sip of water
options.C: Continue metoprolol on schedule and discontinue metformin at least 24 to 48 hours prior to surgery
options.D: Discontinue all medications 24 hours prior to surgery to avoid unpredictable drug interactions
options.E: Withhold metoprolol and atorvastatin, but administer a double dose of metformin on the surgical morning

questions.explanation:
Perioperative pharmacotherapy requires rigorous distinction between drugs that must be strictly maintained to prevent withdrawal crises versus those that must be withheld to avoid life-threatening toxicity.

• Beta-Blockers (Metoprolol): Must be CONTINUED on the morning of surgery with sips of water. Abrupt cessation of chronic beta-blockade causes acute adrenergic receptor upregulation, leading to severe rebound tachycardia, malignant ventricular dysrhythmias, and perioperative myocardial ischemia. Perioperative continuation of beta-blockers reduces overall cardiovascular mortality.
• Biguanides (Metformin): Must be WITHHELD 24 to 48 hours prior to major surgery. Perioperative fasting, anesthesia-induced hypotension, blood loss, and surgical tissue hypoperfusion can trigger acute renal hypoperfusion. Under hypoperfused conditions, metformin inhibits hepatic mitochondrial gluconeogenesis and complex I of the respiratory chain, leading to catastrophic, refractory lactic acidosis with high mortality. Blood glucose is instead managed perioperatively using short-acting insulin.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. Discontinuing chronic beta-blockers preoperatively is dangerous and contraindicated due to rebound sympathetic storm.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Continuing metformin until the morning of surgery places the patient at unacceptable risk of lactic acidosis if intraoperative hypotension or renal hypoperfusion develops.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Chronic beta-blockers should always be continued on the morning of surgery to prevent rebound tachycardia and myocardial ischemia. Metformin must be withheld 24–48 hours preoperatively to prevent fatal lactic acidosis during perioperative hypoperfusion.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. Blanket cessation of all cardiac and pulmonary medications is a dangerous clinical malpractice. Cardiac, anti-hypertensive, and anti-seizure medications should be continued.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. Giving extra metformin in a fasting patient is lethal (severe hypoglycemia and lactic acidosis).

questions.educationalObjective: Chronic beta-blockers should always be continued on the morning of surgery to prevent rebound tachycardia and myocardial ischemia. Metformin must be withheld 24–48 hours preoperatively to prevent fatal lactic acidosis during perioperative hypoperfusion.

questions.question: A 34-year-old woman with severe symptomatic gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and morbid obesity (BMI 42 kg/m<sup>2</sup>) is scheduled for laparoscopic sleeve gastrectomy. She describes severe daily retrosternal burning and water brash despite taking omeprazole. During the preoperative visit, the anesthesiologist formulates an aspiration prophylaxis strategy to prevent Mendelson's syndrome. Which of the following describes the therapeutic mechanism and proper clinical timing of administering oral non-particulate sodium citrate to this patient?

options.A: Ingestion 8 hours preoperatively to permanently suppress parietal cell H<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> ATPase activity
options.B: Administration 2 hours preoperatively to stimulate gastric antral motility and accelerate emptying
options.C: Ingestion of 15 to 30 mL 15 to 30 minutes prior to induction to rapidly neutralize existing gastric acid and elevate pH >2.5
options.D: Injection via intravenous route during induction to prevent histamine-induced bronchospasm
options.E: Ingestion 6 hours preoperatively to inhibit salivary and tracheobronchial gland secretions

questions.explanation:
Mendelson's syndrome (chemical aspiration pneumonitis) develops when gastric fluid with a volume >25 mL (0.4 mL/kg) and a pH <2.5 is aspirated into the tracheobronchial tree, causing severe chemical burn, alveolar-capillary destruction, pulmonary edema, and acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS).

High-risk patients (morbid obesity, GERD, pregnancy, diabetic gastroparesis, hiatal hernia) require multimodal aspiration prophylaxis:
1. Sodium Citrate (0.3 M): A non-particulate liquid antacid administered orally in a volume of 15–30 mL approximately 15 to 30 minutes prior to induction. Because it is already a clear solution, it mixes instantly with residual gastric fluid and immediately buffers gastric hydrochloric acid, raising the gastric pH above the critical danger threshold of 2.5. Unlike particulate antacids (e.g., aluminum/magnesium hydroxide), non-particulate citrate causes minimal pulmonary parenchymal inflammation if accidentally aspirated!
2. H2-Receptor Antagonists / PPIs: Administered several hours prior to surgery to inhibit newly produced acid.
3. Metoclopramide (10 mg IV): Dopamine receptor antagonist given 30–60 minutes preop to enhance gastric emptying and increase lower esophageal sphincter (LES) tone.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. Proton pump inhibitors (omeprazole) inhibit the H<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup> ATPase pump, not sodium citrate. Citrate is a direct chemical buffer.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Enhancing antral motility is the mechanism of prokinetic agents like metoclopramide, not antacids.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Oral non-particulate sodium citrate (15–30 mL) is administered 15 to 30 minutes before anesthesia induction to immediately buffer existing gastric acid, raising pH >2.5 and neutralizing the risk of severe chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson's syndrome) in high-risk patients.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. Sodium citrate is administered strictly orally, not intravenously.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. Drying secretions is the pharmacological effect of anticholinergic agents like glycopyrrolate and atropine.

questions.educationalObjective: Oral non-particulate sodium citrate (15–30 mL) is administered 15 to 30 minutes before anesthesia induction to immediately buffer existing gastric acid, raising pH >2.5 and neutralizing the risk of severe chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson's syndrome) in high-risk patients.

questions.section: Lecture 2: Monitoring in Anesthesia & Physiological Dynamics
questions.question: A 48-year-old female is undergoing an elective 4-hour open reduction and internal fixation of a trimalleolar ankle fracture under general anesthesia with endotracheal intubation. The anesthesia circle breathing system is utilized with a mechanical tidal volume of 500 mL, respiratory rate of 12/min, and fresh gas flow of 1.0 L/min of oxygen. Three hours into the procedure, the anesthesiologist notes that the capnography waveform shows a progressive elevation of the inspiratory baseline (Phase I) above the zero mark, currently reading 8 mmHg. The end-tidal CO<sub>2</sub> (ETCO<sub>2</sub>) has risen from 38 mmHg to 52 mmHg, while the waveform contour itself maintains a normal rectangular morphology with a crisp expiratory upstroke and horizontal plateau. Inspection of the anesthesia workstation reveals that the granules inside the carbon dioxide absorber canister have developed a deep purple discoloration throughout two-thirds of the chamber. Which of the following is the underlying mechanism responsible for this capnographic tracing?

options.A: Exhaustion and saturation of the soda lime carbon dioxide absorber
options.B: Severe acute bronchospasm with air trapping
options.C: Partial accidental extubation with cuff leak
options.D: Acute malignant hyperthermia crisis
options.E: Massive pulmonary thromboembolism

questions.explanation:
In a closed or semi-closed circle anesthesia breathing system, exhaled gas containing CO2 is routed through an absorber canister containing soda lime (calcium hydroxide, sodium hydroxide, and ethyl violet pH indicator dye). The chemical reaction absorbs CO2 and regenerates fresh, CO2-free gas for re-inhalation:

CO2 + H2O → H2CO3
H2CO3 + 2NaOH → Na2CO3 + 2H2O
Na2CO3 + Ca(OH)2 → CaCO3 + 2NaOH

When the chemical capacity of the granules is exhausted, the pH drops below 10.3, triggering ethyl violet dye activation and turning the granules purple. At this point, expired CO2 can no longer be absorbed; it passes unaltered through the canister and is re-inhaled by the patient during inspiration. This results in rebreathing of carbon dioxide, pathognomonically demonstrated on capnography as an elevated inspiratory baseline above zero (>0 mmHg) and a secondary rise in ETCO2.

High-Yield: Management of Soda Lime Exhaustion Intraoperatively
If exhaustion occurs mid-operation and the canister cannot be safely swapped immediately, increase fresh gas flow to >10 L/min (converting the semi-closed circle system into a non-rebreathing system to flush expired CO2 out of the APL valve) until the absorber can be replaced.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. An elevated capnogram baseline above zero mmHg (Phase I > 0) indicates carbon dioxide rebreathing, most commonly caused by exhaustion of the soda lime CO<sub>2</sub> absorber (turning purple) or a faulty expiratory unidirectional valve.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Bronchospasm (asthma/COPD) produces the classic "shark fin" waveform characterized by a slanted, delayed expiratory upstroke and loss of the horizontal plateau. Crucially, the baseline in bronchospasm returns to 0 mmHg during inspiration.
optionExplanations.C: Incorrect. Accidental extubation or a large cuff leak results in sudden loss or drastic attenuation of the capnogram amplitude, dropping toward zero.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. Malignant hyperthermia causes a massive, rapid rise in ETCO<sub>2</sub> due to runaway muscle metabolism, but the inspiratory baseline remains at zero (unless rebreathing secondary to canister exhaustion subsequently occurs).
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. Pulmonary embolism causes a sudden, precipitous drop in ETCO<sub>2</sub> due to acute loss of pulmonary perfusion (increased alveolar dead space), not a rise in baseline.

questions.educationalObjective: An elevated capnogram baseline above zero mmHg (Phase I > 0) indicates carbon dioxide rebreathing, most commonly caused by exhaustion of the soda lime CO<sub>2</sub> absorber (turning purple) or a faulty expiratory unidirectional valve.

questions.section: Lecture 2: Monitoring in Anesthesia & Physiological Dynamics
questions.question: A 67-year-old male with a history of prior anterior wall myocardial infarction and type 2 diabetes mellitus is scheduled for elective open right hemicolectomy under general anesthesia. The anesthesiologist configures a 5-lead electrocardiographic monitoring system in the operating room. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the specific clinical utility of Lead II and Lead V5 during intraoperative cardiac monitoring?

options.A: Lead II is the single most sensitive lead for detecting left ventricular subendocardial ischemia
options.B: Simultaneous monitoring of Lead II and V5 detects less than 50% of intraoperative ischemic events
options.C: Lead II is optimal for rhythm and P-wave identification, while combining Lead II and Lead V5 detects over 85% of ischemic episodes
options.D: The TP interval represents the correct reference level for measuring ST-segment deviation
options.E: Lead V5 electrode should be placed in the 4th intercostal space at the right sternal border

questions.explanation:
Electrocardiographic monitoring in the operating room serves two distinct, crucial objectives: detection of cardiac dysrhythmias and detection of myocardial ischemia.

• Bipolar Lead II: The electrical axis of Lead II (parallel to the normal anatomical vector of atrial depolarization from SA node to AV node) provides the largest, most distinct P-waves, making it the superior lead for distinguishing normal sinus rhythm from junctional rhythms, atrial fibrillation, flutter, and heart blocks.
• Precordial Lead V5: Located at the 5th intercostal space in the anterior axillary line, Lead V5 views the bulky anterolateral left ventricular myocardium. It is the single most sensitive lead for detecting ischemic ST-segment depression or elevation.
• Combined Surveillance: Clinical trials have established that monitoring Lead II alone detects ~33% of ischemic episodes, Lead V5 alone detects ~75%, but combining Lead II and Lead V5 detects over 85% to 90% of all intraoperative ischemic events!

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. Lead V5 (not Lead II) is the single most sensitive lead for left ventricular ischemia. Lead II monitors the inferior wall and is best for rhythm analysis.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. The combination of Lead II and V5 detects >85% of ischemic events, far exceeding 50%.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Lead II is superior for P-wave identification and dysrhythmia detection, whereas Lead V5 is most sensitive for left ventricular ischemia. Simultaneous monitoring of Lead II and Lead V5 detects over 85% of all intraoperative ischemic events.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. The correct reference baseline for measuring ST-segment elevation or depression is the PR segment, NOT the TP interval! Tachycardia causes the P-wave to merge with the preceding T-wave, obliterating the TP interval.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. The 4th intercostal space at the right sternal border is the anatomical location for V1, not V5. V5 is placed at the 5th intercostal space, anterior axillary line.

questions.educationalObjective: Lead II is superior for P-wave identification and dysrhythmia detection, whereas Lead V5 is most sensitive for left ventricular ischemia. Simultaneous monitoring of Lead II and Lead V5 detects over 85% of all intraoperative ischemic events.

questions.question: A 65-year-old male with severe septic shock secondary to perforated diverticulitis is brought to the operating room for emergency exploratory laparotomy. The anesthesiologist places a triple-lumen central venous catheter via the right internal jugular vein. The pressure transducer is zeroed at the phlebostatic axis, and the monitor displays a central venous pressure (CVP) of 4 mmHg. Regarding the physiological information provided by central venous pressure monitoring, which of the following statements is FALSE?

options.A: CVP provides an estimate of right atrial pressure and right ventricular preload
options.B: Serial trends in CVP and hemodynamic responses to fluid challenges are more informative than a single static value
options.C: The right internal jugular vein is anatomically favored over the left due to a short, direct, straight course into the superior vena cava
options.D: CVP monitoring directly measures left atrial pressure and left ventricular end-diastolic performance
options.E: Inadvertent arterial puncture and pneumothorax are recognized complications of internal jugular vein cannulation

questions.explanation:
Central venous catheterization places a catheter tip at the junction of the superior vena cava and the right atrium. Therefore, CVP directly measures Right Atrial Pressure (RAP) and right ventricular end-diastolic filling pressure (RV preload).

CVP DOES NOT measure left atrial pressure or left ventricular end-diastolic performance. In healthy individuals without cardiopulmonary pathology, RV filling may roughly correlate with LV filling, but in patients with pulmonary hypertension, left ventricular dysfunction, mitral valve disease, or sepsis, right-sided pressures completely dissociate from left-sided hemodynamics. Direct measurement of left atrial pressure requires a pulmonary artery catheter (Swan-Ganz) to record Pulmonary Capillary Wedge Pressure (PCWP).

optionExplanations.A: True statement, so not the answer to this question. CVP is the driving pressure for filling the right atrium and right ventricle.
optionExplanations.B: True statement, so not the answer to this question. Dynamic fluid challenges (infusing 250–500 mL of crystalloid and observing CVP, stroke volume, and blood pressure response) are far more predictive of volume responsiveness than any single static CVP number.
optionExplanations.C: True statement, so not the answer to this question. The right internal jugular vein has a straight, direct path into the SVC, whereas the left IJV enters the left brachiocephalic vein at an acute angle and crosses the thoracic duct.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Central venous pressure (CVP) monitoring provides an estimate of right atrial pressure and right ventricular preload only; it does NOT measure left atrial pressure or left ventricular end-diastolic performance.
optionExplanations.E: True statement, so not the answer to this question. Carotid puncture (located medial and slightly posterior to the IJV) and pneumothorax are well-documented mechanical complications of IJV access.

questions.educationalObjective: Central venous pressure (CVP) monitoring provides an estimate of right atrial pressure and right ventricular preload only; it does NOT measure left atrial pressure or left ventricular end-diastolic performance.

questions.question: A 24-year-old male is intubated following rapid sequence induction for an emergency laparotomy. The endotracheal tube is taped at 26 cm at the incisors. Mechanical ventilation is initiated, and the capnograph displays a continuous, robust, rectangular CO<sub>2</sub> waveform with an ETCO<sub>2</sub> of 38 mmHg. Pulse oximetry reads 99%. However, 15 minutes later, peak inspiratory airway pressure rises from 18 cmH<sub>2</sub>O to 34 cmH<sub>2</sub>O. Physical examination reveals diminished breath sounds over the left hemithorax and vigorous chest expansion over the right hemithorax. Auscultation confirms bilateral epigastric silence. Which of the following clinical conditions CANNOT be reliably detected or ruled out by capnography alone?

options.A: Complete breathing circuit disconnection
options.B: Accidental esophageal intubation
options.C: Endobronchial (mainstem) intubation
options.D: Acute severe bronchospasm
options.E: Return of spontaneous ventilation during mechanical paralysis

questions.explanation:
Capnography is the universally recognized gold standard for confirming that an endotracheal tube is positioned within the tracheobronchial tree (ruling out esophageal intubation). However, capnography CANNOT detect endobronchial (mainstem) intubation!

When an endotracheal tube is advanced too deeply into a mainstem bronchus (most commonly the right mainstem bronchus due to its wider diameter and more vertical takeoff), exhaled gas from the intubated lung still contains alveolar CO2. The capnograph samples this gas normally, producing a completely normal-appearing rectangular waveform and a normal ETCO2 value. Capnography is blind to whether one lung or two lungs are being ventilated!

Endobronchial intubation can only be diagnosed clinically by auscultation of breath sounds bilaterally in both axillae and anterior lung fields, observing symmetric chest excursion, or confirming tube depth via chest radiography or fiberoptic bronchoscopy.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. Circuit disconnection causes immediate loss of CO<sub>2</sub> sensing, producing a sudden flatline (ETCO<sub>2</sub> = 0) with an audible disconnect alarm.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Esophageal intubation is immediately ruled out by sustained, normal capnographic waveforms across ≥5 breaths. (In esophageal intubation, small amounts of swallowed CO<sub>2</sub> may appear for 1–2 breaths, but quickly decays to zero).
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Capnography confirms tracheal placement versus esophageal intubation, but it CANNOT detect endobronchial (mainstem) intubation. Bilateral auscultation of breath sounds is essential to verify correct depth above the carina.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. Bronchospasm creates a distinctive, pathognomonic "shark fin" waveform with a prolonged, upward-sloping expiratory plateau.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. Spontaneous diaphragmatic efforts breaking through neuromuscular blockade produce a characteristic "curare cleft" in the Phase III plateau.

questions.educationalObjective: Capnography confirms tracheal placement versus esophageal intubation, but it CANNOT detect endobronchial (mainstem) intubation. Bilateral auscultation of breath sounds is essential to verify correct depth above the carina.

questions.question: A 35-year-old male is undergoing an emergency exploratory laparotomy for a gunshot wound to the abdomen under general anesthesia with rocuronium muscle relaxation. During manipulation of the mesentery, the anesthesiologist observes that the patient's blood pressure rises from 115/70 mmHg to 165/105 mmHg, heart rate accelerates from 70 bpm to 118 bpm, and profuse diaphoresis and tearing from both eyes are noted. The patient is completely motionless with 0 twitches on train-of-four monitoring. Which of the following statements regarding the depth of anesthesia in this patient is correct?

options.A: The patient is in an excessively deep plane of anesthesia characterized by parasympathetic surge
options.B: Bradycardia and hypotension are the classic autonomic hallmarks of light anesthesia under muscle relaxants
options.C: Tachycardia, hypertension, lacrimation, and sweating are pathognomonic signs of inadequate depth of anesthesia in a paralyzed patient
options.D: Somatic motor movement is the only reliable indicator of inadequate anesthesia in paralyzed patients
options.E: Increasing the dose of muscle relaxants is the primary treatment for these autonomic signs

questions.explanation:
In an unparalyzed patient, inadequate depth of anesthesia (light anesthesia) is readily recognized by somatic motor responses: facial grimacing, eye opening, swallowing, and purposeful movements of the limbs.

However, when a patient is fully pharmacologically paralyzed with neuromuscular blocking agents (such as rocuronium), all somatic motor responses are abolished (0 twitches on train-of-four). In this paralyzed state, the conscious brain retains autonomic sympathetic reflexes to painful surgical stimulation. Inadequate anesthesia is signaled exclusively by autonomic sympathetic hyperactivity:
• Tachycardia & Systemic Hypertension
• Lacrimation (tearing from the eyes)
• Diaphoresis (sweating on the forehead/palms)
• Pupillary dilation (mydriasis)

Administering additional muscle relaxants in this setting is a classic malpractice trap; it paralyzes the patient further while leaving them conscious and in agony! The proper intervention is to immediately deepen the hypnotic/ anesthetic agent (e.g., increase volatile gas concentration or IV propofol) and administer adequate analgesia (e.g., IV fentanyl).

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. Excessive anesthesia causes profound cardiovascular depression, manifesting as hypotension, bradycardia, and myocardial depression.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Bradycardia and hypotension are signs of deep anesthesia, not light anesthesia.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. In patients paralyzed with neuromuscular blockers, inadequate depth of anesthesia manifests as sympathetic hyperactivity: hypertension, tachycardia, lacrimation, and diaphoresis. Deepening hypnosis and analgesia is the mandatory response.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. Paralyzed patients cannot move; autonomic signs are the primary monitoring modality.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. Giving more muscle relaxant does not treat awareness or pain; it only suppresses movement and increases the trauma of intraoperative recall.

questions.educationalObjective: In patients paralyzed with neuromuscular blockers, inadequate depth of anesthesia manifests as sympathetic hyperactivity: hypertension, tachycardia, lacrimation, and diaphoresis. Deepening hypnosis and analgesia is the mandatory response.

questions.question: A 72-year-old female with a history of deep vein thrombosis is undergoing an elective total hip replacement under general anesthesia. Two hours into surgery, during reaming of the femoral canal, the end-tidal CO<sub>2</sub> (ETCO<sub>2</sub>) monitor alarms, showing an abrupt drop from 38 mmHg to 14 mmHg. Mechanical ventilation parameters remain unchanged at a tidal volume of 450 mL and respiratory rate of 12/min with confirmed bilateral chest rise and breath sounds. Her blood pressure drops acutely from 120/75 mmHg to 72/40 mmHg, and heart rate increases from 75 bpm to 125 bpm. An urgent arterial blood gas (ABG) analysis reveals a PaO<sub>2</sub> of 58 mmHg and a PaCO<sub>2</sub> of 48 mmHg on an FiO<sub>2</sub> of 0.60. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the sudden drop in ETCO<sub>2</sub> in this patient?

options.A: Acute severe hyperthermia crisis
options.B: Endobronchial intubation into the right mainstem bronchus
options.C: Acute massive pulmonary embolism with increased alveolar dead space
options.D: Accidental intravenous sodium bicarbonate administration
options.E: Saturated soda lime canister in the circle system

questions.explanation:
End-tidal carbon dioxide (ETCO2) is determined by three physiological factors: (1) cellular CO2 production, (2) pulmonary capillary blood flow (cardiac output), and (3) alveolar minute ventilation.

When a patient suffers an acute pulmonary embolism (thrombus, bone marrow fat, or air), emboli lodge in the pulmonary arterial tree, acutely occluding pulmonary blood flow to large segments of the lung parenchyma. While these alveoli continue to receive mechanical ventilation, they receive no perfusion. This creates massive alveolar dead space (high V/Q mismatch):
• Expired gas from unperfused alveoli contains 0 mmHg CO2, which severely dilutes the small amount of CO2 exiting perfused lung units.
• This causes an immediate, dramatic collapse in measured ETCO2 (dropping from 38 to 14 mmHg).
• Concurrently, CO2 cannot escape the systemic circulation, causing arterial blood CO2 to rise, creating a wide arterial-to-end-tidal CO2 gradient (PaCO2 − ETCO2 = 48 − 14 = 34 mmHg; normal is 2–5 mmHg)!
• The acute obstruction to right ventricular outflow causes acute RV strain, tachycardia, and severe hypotension.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. Hyperthermia (and malignant hyperthermia) increases metabolic rate and CO<sub>2</sub> production, resulting in a dramatic elevation of ETCO<sub>2</sub> (>50–70 mmHg).
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Mainstem intubation ventilates one lung adequately, which continues to exhale normal alveolar CO<sub>2</sub> (~35–40 mmHg). It does not cause a collapse of ETCO<sub>2</sub> to 14 mmHg.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A sudden, precipitous drop in end-tidal CO<sub>2</sub> accompanied by acute hypotension and tachycardia is a hallmark of acute pulmonary embolism, caused by an abrupt increase in alveolar dead space (ventilated but unperfused alveoli) and an expanded PaCO<sub>2</sub>–ETCO<sub>2</sub> gradient.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. IV sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO<sub>3</sub>) reacts with hydrogen ions to produce carbonic acid, which dissociates into CO<sub>2</sub> and water, transiently elevating ETCO<sub>2</sub>.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. Exhausted soda lime causes CO<sub>2</sub> rebreathing, producing an increase in ETCO<sub>2</sub> and an elevated baseline above zero.

questions.educationalObjective: A sudden, precipitous drop in end-tidal CO<sub>2</sub> accompanied by acute hypotension and tachycardia is a hallmark of acute pulmonary embolism, caused by an abrupt increase in alveolar dead space (ventilated but unperfused alveoli) and an expanded PaCO<sub>2</sub>–ETCO<sub>2</sub> gradient.

questions.question: A 52-year-old male is undergoing an open cholecystectomy under general endotracheal anesthesia. Two hours into the operation, while the patient is mechanically ventilated at a fixed rate of 10 breaths/min, the anesthesiologist notices an indentation or saddle-shaped "notch" appearing in the latter third of the alveolar plateau (Phase III) on the capnography monitor. The depth of this notch progressively deepens over several breaths, though the baseline remains at 0 mmHg. No alarms are triggered on the anesthesia machine. Which of the following does this capnographic tracing indicate?

options.A: Inadvertent development of tension pneumothorax
options.B: Sclerosis and water condensation inside the sampling tubing
options.C: Return of spontaneous diaphragmatic efforts as muscle relaxant effect wanes (Curare Cleft)
options.D: Acute incompetence of the circle system inhalation check valve
options.E: Acute severe cardiogenic pulmonary edema

questions.explanation:
The appearance of a dip, notch, or cleft in the flat alveolar plateau (Phase III) of the capnogram is known clinically as a Curare Cleft.

A curare cleft is the pathognomonic capnographic hallmark of spontaneous diaphragmatic contraction attempting to breathe during controlled mechanical ventilation. As the pharmacological concentration of neuromuscular blocking agent (muscle relaxant) declines at the neuromuscular junction, the diaphragm— being the most resistant respiratory muscle to paralysis and the first to recover—begins making brief, uncoordinated inspiratory twitches against the mechanical ventilator. This brief inspiratory twitch draws fresh, CO2-free gas into the airway, momentarily diluting expired CO2 and producing a sharp dip in the alveolar plateau.

The depth of the curare cleft is inversely proportional to the degree of neuromuscular blockade (a deeper notch indicates more recovery of spontaneous diaphragmatic strength). It serves as an early visual alert that the patient requires additional muscle relaxants to maintain surgical stillness or, near the end of surgery, that the patient is preparing for pharmacological reversal and extubation.

optionExplanations.A: Incorrect. Pneumothorax causes high peak inspiratory pressures, loss of breath sounds, and potentially hemodynamic collapse, but does not produce an isolated notch in the plateau.
optionExplanations.B: Incorrect. Water condensation in the sidestream sampling tube causes high-frequency oscillations or complete occlusion with an "airway obstructed" error.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A curare cleft is an indentation in the alveolar plateau (Phase III) of the capnogram that signals spontaneous diaphragmatic breathing efforts as neuromuscular blockade wears off. Its depth is inversely proportional to the degree of residual muscle relaxation.
optionExplanations.D: Incorrect. Incompetence of check valves causes rebreathing with an elevated Phase I baseline above zero.
optionExplanations.E: Incorrect. Pulmonary edema causes hypoxemia, coarse crackles, and copious pink frothy sputum; it does not produce a curare cleft.

questions.educationalObjective: A curare cleft is an indentation in the alveolar plateau (Phase III) of the capnogram that signals spontaneous diaphragmatic breathing efforts as neuromuscular blockade wears off. Its depth is inversely proportional to the degree of residual muscle relaxation.
